You may come across charts that sort the world into regions and describe how people in each supposedly communicate or lead. Most of them draw on cluster frameworks, and the best known of these comes from the GLOBE research program, a large international study of culture and leadership. GLOBE researchers surveyed roughly seventeen thousand managers in about sixty societies about the practices and values they saw in their organizations and societies. They then grouped societies whose responses were similar. A study by Vipin Gupta, Paul Hanges and Peter Dorfman tested proposed groupings statistically and found support for ten clusters: Anglo, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Latin Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Arab (named Middle East in some later GLOBE writing), South Asia and Confucian Asia.

Cluster studies can provide historical context for questions about organizations and societies. They cannot predict the preferences, behavior or needs of any individual. One separate overview of cultural clusters is David Livermore’s Expand Your Borders (2013). The groupings in this course are described by the GLOBE research program.

It is just as important to know what the data did not measure. The respondents were managers in organizations, not a cross-section of each society. The results are averages for societies, usually countries, not descriptions of individuals. They were collected at a particular time, and societies change. Many people and peoples do not fit national boundaries: the Hmong live across several countries, Dakota and Anishinaabe nations are sovereign nations within what is now Minnesota, and many Minnesotans have heritage in more than one society or grew up here with parents from elsewhere. Religious, linguistic, regional and class differences within a country do not show up in a national average. Introductory textbooks that teach GLOBE make the same point, warning that relying solely on such frameworks can be misleading.

So hold two ideas together. Cluster research is real, careful work that can help you notice patterns, including your own. And a cluster describes a statistical tendency across a group of societies. Clusters say nothing about any person, and they say nothing about Minnesota communities. They were not built from Minnesota residents, and they cannot tell you how the person on the other side of the table communicates, decides or builds trust. To learn about a community here, go to the program’s community briefs and to the people themselves. The rest of this course is about using the map without mistaking it for the territory.

Cultural intelligence in this program is a broad, multidisciplinary practice of learning and working across differences. Sociology, anthropology, psychology, education, communication and other fields offer different questions; disability justice, person-centered practice, intercultural development and psychological safety add further perspectives. No single model defines the entire program.

Regional research can offer historical context, but group averages cannot tell us what an individual thinks, needs or prefers. Ask people what matters to them, consider their choices and access needs, and check assumptions against evidence.

Also examine organizational power: who sets the rules, whose knowledge counts, who can participate and whether policies create unequal barriers. Curiosity and flexible communication matter, but individual intentions alone do not resolve structural inequity.

Learning and reflection can support change, but this course does not assign a score, predict outcomes or replace agency responsibilities.

This program uses cultural intelligence to mean learning and working across differences. It draws on several fields, including sociology, anthropology, psychology, education and communication. Disability justice, person-centered practice, intercultural development and psychological safety offer further perspectives. No single model defines the whole program. Ang and colleagues studied a specific model with four dimensions, often called CQ. That research does not establish that every approach used here is the same or has the same evidence.

Regional research offers limited context. Group averages cannot establish what a person thinks, needs or prefers. Ask what matters to the person, consider their choices and access needs, and check your assumptions against evidence.

Look at power within the organization too. Who sets the rules? Whose knowledge counts? Who can take part, and what barriers do policies create? Curiosity and flexible communication can help, but good intentions alone do not resolve unequal access.

Reflection can support learning. This course does not assign a score, predict someone’s performance or replace agency duties. More comments after a meeting may show that another way to contribute was useful. That change alone does not establish psychological safety or explain why someone was quiet before. changes.before:
The ecological fallacy is the error of assuming that relationships observed for groups necessarily hold for individuals. The statistician David Freedman explained it with a classic example: finding higher suicide rates in societies with more Protestants does not show that Protestants themselves were more likely to die by suicide. Group data and individual data answer different questions. A pattern across groups can even reverse when you look at individuals.

Cluster frameworks are group data. If the average response from one cluster's managers leaned toward respect for hierarchy, that tells you something about the societies in that cluster compared with others. It does not tell you whether a particular colleague who grew up in one of those societies prefers a hierarchical style. The spread of individuals within a society is usually wide, and the averages of two societies can differ while many individuals from each overlap. Add migration, generation, profession, faith, disability, personal history and the organizational culture of DHS itself, and the distance between a society's average and one person's style grows further.

In practice, the ecological fallacy shows up in small moments. A hiring panelist reads a candidate's hesitation to self-promote as a cultural trait rather than asking a follow-up question. A supervisor assumes a new employee from a certain region will not want to disagree in meetings and stops inviting their view. A case manager assumes a family from a particular country will not want outside help. Each takes a real pattern and applies it to a person who never had a chance to show whether it fits. Stereotypes are often built this way: not from invented facts, but from true averages misapplied.

A group pattern may suggest a question or a change to a system, but it never predicts the person in front of you. Offer accessible options, ask the person and respect their choices. Decisions with real consequences must follow the relevant facts and responsible process.

If you do use a cluster pattern, and you never have to, how should you use it? The answer is to turn it into a question you ask, never an expectation of the person. This is the planning, awareness and checking part of cultural intelligence. It uses knowledge to widen what you prepare for, rather than narrow what you expect.

A simple sequence works well. First, name the pattern: "Research suggests societies in this cluster tended, on average, to place more emphasis on relationships before business." Second, turn it on yourself: what is my own default here, and what would I miss if the meeting ran only that way? If you are used to getting straight to the agenda, that is also a cultural pattern, and it may be the one that needs adjusting. Third, list the options you can offer: a clear agenda, time for introductions for those who want it, and more than one way to contribute. Fourth, ask, and let the person choose: "How would you like to use our time today?" Fifth, revise: what the person tells you replaces the pattern. Then, importantly, do not carry that person's preference onto the next person from the same region.

One further habit keeps those questions honest: look beyond national culture. DHS has its own organizational culture, professions have norms, disability communities have cultures, and generations differ. A county social worker and a state policy analyst from the same background may still work very differently.

Consider how assumptions about communication, time, decision-making and authority shape your own habits, your team and its processes. These questions are not labels for people or communities.

In DHS and DSD work, this approach has a narrow use: noticing your own defaults and widening what you prepare for. It tells you nothing about a Minnesota community or the person you are meeting. To learn about them, go to the program's community briefs, community partners and the people served. It never justifies treating someone differently in a formal decision. A framework can remind you to prepare for more than one style. The people you work with give you the answers.
